For accelerationists, this expert optimism validates the case that AI's transformative potential is real and recognized by those with the deepest knowledge. This strong personal benefit expectation among experts reinforces the accelerationist claim that AI creates real, tangible value for those who work with it. The contrast with the general public (24% benefit vs. 43% harm) underscores that expert proximity to AI correlates with optimism. This normative commitment to AI-enhanced work is a core accelerationist aspiration.

key_points.point: AI experts believe AI will have large positive impacts across multiple domains including the economy, medical care, and education, reflecting the accelerationist belief that AI can tackle complex, society-wide problems. The survey documents large gaps between expert and public views on these domains. Experts see AI as a broadly beneficial force across sectors. key_points.excerpt_context: Key findings section, page 8

This belief supports the accelerationist view that AI is already deeply embedded in daily life and is a pervasive, transformative force. Only 27% of the public self-reports this level of interaction, suggesting a gap between actual AI exposure and public awareness. This belief underpins accelerationist arguments that AI adoption is already advanced.

key_points.excerpt_context: Chapter 1, page 19-20

key_points.point: AI experts report that chatbots are extremely or very helpful to them at a rate of 61%, far higher than the 33% of general public chatbot users who say the same. This supports the accelerationist belief that AI tools deliver substantial practical value, especially to those with expertise to use them effectively. The gap suggests that AI's benefits are real but may require expertise to unlock. This is consistent with the accelerationist view of AI as a powerful productivity tool.
key_points.verbatim: About six-in-ten AI experts who have used a chatbot (61%) say it was extremely or very helpful to them. Smaller shares of users in the general public (33%) say this.
key_points.excerpt_context: Chapter 1, page 21-22

key_points.point: The document reports that only 18% of experts and 10% of the public believe AI will positively affect news, with about half or more of both groups predicting negative effects. This challenges accelerationist narratives about AI democratizing information and improving public discourse. The near-consensus pessimism on news and elections among experts is notable given their general optimism about economic and productivity impacts. This suggests even accelerationist-leaning experts draw sharp distinctions between domains.

key_points.point: 56% of AI experts believe AI's impact on the U.S. over the next 20 years will be positive, while only 15% say it will be negative. This majority-positive expert forecast supports the accelerationist view that AI will deliver net benefits at a societal scale. The data further shows that male experts (63%) are more optimistic than female experts (36%), and those at private companies (63%) match university-based experts (55%) in positivity. The 20-year timeframe aligns with accelerationist narratives about transformative long-run gains.

key_points.point: AI experts, by virtue of their professional identity and proximity to the technology, implicitly advocate for AI's continued development and deployment by expressing strong optimism about its benefits. The survey captures this as a revealed preference — experts are more excited than concerned (47% vs. 15% of the public). This enthusiasm functions as an implicit argument for accelerating AI development. The caveat is that even experts want more regulation and control, tempering pure accelerationism.
key_points.verbatim: And while 47% of experts surveyed say they are more excited than concerned about the increased use of AI in daily life, that share drops to 11% among the public.
key_points.excerpt_context: Key findings section, page 7

key_points.point: Despite their optimism, AI experts join the public in wanting more control over AI and worrying about insufficient government regulation, which cuts against a pure accelerationist stance of minimal oversight. More than half of experts (57%) want more control over how AI is used in their lives. This suggests even accelerationist-leaning experts see a role for governance. The document frames this as common ground between experts and the public.
key_points.verbatim: More than half of U.S. adults (55%) and a similar share of AI experts (57%) say they want more control over how it is used in their lives. And those in both groups worry more that government regulation of AI will be too lax than overly excessive.
key_points.excerpt_context: Key findings section, page 8

key_points.point: The document reports that 74% of AI experts believe AI will make humans more productive over the next 20 years, a figure far exceeding public confidence at 17%. This expert consensus reflects the accelerationist belief that AI is already delivering and will continue to deliver measurable productivity gains. The gap between expert and public views suggests that those closest to the technology are most convinced of its transformative economic potential. The caveat is that this is a predictive belief, not a documented outcome.

key_points.excerpt_context: Section 3, page 48, paragraph on productivity predictions

These figures reflect the accelerationist belief that AI can tackle complex, high-stakes information problems in critical sectors. The 40-percentage-point gap between experts and the public on medical care is particularly striking. The caveat is that these are forward-looking predictions from a self-selected expert sample.

key_points.excerpt_context: Section 3, page 41-42, paragraph on health care and education views

This aligns with the accelerationist belief that new technology creates new kinds of work. However, the document also records an expert quote explicitly questioning whether new jobs will match displaced ones, which complicates this reading.

This reflects the accelerationist view that AI augments human work by handling routine tasks. This nuanced accelerationist position supports AI's current economic value without overstating its capabilities. The expert frames AI as a 'very good product' for productivity improvement. key_points.point: The document reports that roughly half of AI experts surveyed think AI will one day reach a point where they would trust it to make important decisions for them, compared with only 13% of the general public. This reflects an accelerationist belief that AI capabilities will mature to the point of reliable, expert-level decision support. The gender gap within experts (58% of men vs. 30% of women) adds nuance. The caveat is that 'trust' is a subjective measure and does not specify the domain of decisions.

This finding directly challenges the accelerationist vision of AI-driven abundance leading to improved human well-being. Even among the most AI-optimistic group, happiness gains are not widely anticipated. This is a significant caveat to accelerationist claims about AI's societal benefits.

key_points.excerpt_context: Section 3, page 48-49, paragraph on AI and human happiness

key_points.point: The document reports that only 11% of AI experts and 9% of the public believe AI will positively impact elections, with 61% of experts believing AI will harm elections. This finding strongly contradicts accelerationist claims about AI as a broadly beneficial force for society. Even domain experts who are optimistic about AI's economic and productivity impacts are deeply pessimistic about its effects on democratic institutions. This represents a significant internal tension within expert opinion.

This rising awareness trend supports the accelerationist narrative that AI is becoming an increasingly central technology in public consciousness. Greater public familiarity could translate into broader adoption and acceptance of AI-driven solutions. The data does not, however, indicate whether increased awareness correlates with more positive or negative attitudes.

key_points.point: Both experts and the public want more personal control over AI in their lives, with 55% of adults and 57% of experts expressing this desire. This reflects the safetyist concern that AI deployment is outpacing individual agency and consent. The document presents this as a cross-group consensus. The desire for control is linked to broader concerns about lax oversight.

key_points.excerpt_context: Key findings section, page 8

key_points.point: Both experts and the public recognize that AI design underrepresents the perspectives of women, Black, and Hispanic adults, reflecting the safetyist concern that AI systems encode and perpetuate historical injustices. The document notes that 75% of experts say men's perspectives are well-represented, but only 44% say the same for women. This disparity is seen as a structural problem in AI development. Expert quotes reinforce that underrepresented groups will be disproportionately harmed by AI.

This safetyist belief holds that industry self-regulation is insufficient. The document notes that academic experts are far more skeptical of industry than industry experts themselves (60% vs. 39% lacking confidence). An expert quote explicitly states that corporate responsibility does not drive decision-making on AI release timelines.

key_points.point: Bias in AI decision-making is a shared concern for both experts and the public, with 55% of each group highly concerned. This reflects the safetyist belief that AI systems can cause systematic harm through discriminatory outputs. The document connects this to hiring algorithms and medical decision-making as specific high-stakes domains. Expert quotes reinforce that underrepresented groups will be first to suffer from AI-driven displacement.
key_points.verbatim: Bias in decisions made by AI is also a concern for experts and the public (55% each say they're highly concerned).
key_points.excerpt_context: Key findings / Concerns section, page 13

key_points.point: Inaccurate information from AI is a top concern for both experts (70%) and the public (66%), reflecting the safetyist belief that AI systems pose risks through misinformation and unreliable outputs. This is one of the highest-concern items in the survey. The document frames this as a shared worry cutting across expert and public divides. Impersonation and data misuse are also common worries.

key_points.excerpt_context: Key findings / Concerns section, page 13

key_points.point: Academic AI experts are far more skeptical of corporate responsibility than their industry peers, with 60% of university-based experts lacking confidence in companies versus 39% of private-sector experts. This reflects the safetyist belief that those closest to commercial incentives are least likely to prioritize safety. The document presents this sector gap as a significant finding. It suggests that institutional position shapes risk perception.
key_points.verbatim: 60% of experts at colleges or universities have little to no confidence that companies will develop and use AI responsibly. 39% of those at private companies or businesses say the same.
key_points.excerpt_context: Regulation section, page 17

key_points.point: AI companies are attempting to address racial and gender bias through improved training methods and workforce diversity, but these efforts face pushback as companies scale back diversity initiatives. This reflects the safetyist concern that bias mitigation is fragile and subject to corporate reversal. The document presents this as an ongoing tension in AI development. The rollback of diversity efforts is framed as a risk factor for perpetuating bias.
key_points.verbatim: One way AI companies are dealing with potential racial and gender biases in their models is by improving how models are trained. There are also growing calls for more diverse workforces to counteract bias. These efforts, though, have been met with pushback as companies scale back these initiatives.
key_points.excerpt_context: Bias and representation section, page 13

key_points.point: The Pew Research Center designed this study to systematically compare public and expert views on AI risks and opportunities, functioning as a proactive effort to map societal concerns before harms fully materialize. The methodology — surveying 5,410 adults and 1,013 experts — reflects an intention to generate evidence for governance decisions. This is consistent with the safetyist approach of studying AI's societal impacts before widespread deployment. The study explicitly covers employment, bias, regulation, and democratic processes.

This report includes findings from a survey of U.S. adults, a survey of AI experts and a series of in-depth interviews with experts.

The quote frames corporate irresponsibility as a structural feature of industry incentives, not an exception. This supports safetyist arguments for mandatory pre-deployment review. The speaker is identified as working at a private company, making the critique particularly notable.

This reflects the safetyist intention to center vulnerable populations in AI risk analysis. The quotes connect workforce diversity to AI safety outcomes. This framing argues that homogeneous AI development teams create systemic risks for marginalized communities.

This aligns with safetyist concerns about AI-driven skill decay in high-expertise fields. The document notes that 38% of AI experts predict fewer lawyer jobs, compared with 23% of the public, indicating experts see greater risk to knowledge-work professions. The caveat is that this is a job-count prediction, not a direct measure of skill atrophy.

key_points.excerpt_context: Section 3, page 46, paragraph on occupational impacts

key_points.point: The Pew Research Center survey itself embodies the safetyist intention of proactively studying AI's long-term societal impacts before widespread deployment consequences are fully realized. The survey examines AI's predicted effects across 10 sectors over a 20-year horizon, including employment, health care, education, elections, and the environment. This systematic, evidence-gathering approach reflects the safetyist commitment to anticipating harms. The caveat is that the survey measures opinions, not outcomes.

This is relevant to safetyist discourse because it suggests the expert community does not view transformative AI risk as imminent on a 20-year horizon. However, 40% of the public believes independent AI thought will be possible, indicating significant public concern about this scenario. The safetyist implication is that public fear may outpace expert assessment of near-term risk.

While the expert community is less alarmed than the public (35% of whom expect major harm), a non-trivial share of domain experts still anticipates serious harm. This finding is relevant to safetyist discourse as it shows that catastrophic risk concerns are not confined to the general public but are held by a meaningful minority of technical experts. The caveat is that 'major harm' is undefined in the survey.

U.S. adults are more likely than experts to believe AI will cause major harm to humans (35% vs. 20%). Meanwhile, 46% of experts say this is unlikely, compared with 18% of adults overall.

key_points.point: The document's methodology section reveals that the expert sample was drawn from AI conference authors and presenters, a population that skews toward those already embedded in the AI ecosystem. This sampling approach may underrepresent experts with more critical or cautionary views, potentially inflating optimism in the expert survey results. Safetyists would note this as a limitation in assessing the true distribution of expert concern about AI risks. The document itself acknowledges that expert views are only representative of those who responded.

key_points.point: The document reports near-consensus pessimism among AI experts about AI's impact on elections, with 61% predicting harm. This is one of the strongest findings in the section and aligns with safetyist concerns about AI enabling disinformation, manipulation, and erosion of democratic institutions. The fact that domain experts — not just the general public — hold this view lends credibility to the concern. This finding cuts across the general expert optimism about AI's economic benefits.

With 28% not sure, the criminal justice domain shows both significant concern and significant uncertainty. For safetyists, this data reflects public awareness that AI in criminal justice can perpetuate or amplify existing injustices, a concern well-documented in algorithmic accountability research. key_points.point: About three-quarters of both U.S. adults and AI experts believe AI will lead to fewer jobs for cashiers over the next 20 years, and about half or more say the same for journalists, software engineers, and factory workers. This represents rare expert-public consensus on specific occupational displacement. The document presents this as empirical common ground across otherwise divergent groups. The finding grounds abstract job-loss fears in specific, named occupations.
key_points.verbatim: About three-quarters of U.S. adults and AI experts alike say that over the next 20 years, AI will lead to fewer jobs of this kind in the U.S. About half or more also say this for journalists, software engineers and factory workers.
key_points.excerpt_context: AI and jobs section, page 11-12

key_points.point: Bias in AI decision-making is a high-concern issue for 55% of both experts and the public, with specific reference to hiring algorithms and medical decision-making as domains where bias causes real harm. The document connects this to race, ethnicity, and gender as the primary axes of discrimination. This reflects the skeptic belief that AI systems produce documented, measurable discriminatory outcomes. The mention of hiring and medical contexts grounds the concern in high-stakes real-world applications.
key_points.verbatim: Bias in decisions made by AI is also a concern for experts and the public (55% each say they're highly concerned). Race, ethnicity and gender often dominate discussions on AI, bias and discrimination — from hiring algorithms to medical decision-making.
key_points.excerpt_context: Concerns / Bias section, page 13

key_points.point: Among the U.S. public, only 19% believe AI designers take Black adults' perspectives into account well, while 38% say they do not. This public perception of racial bias in AI design aligns with documented evidence of algorithmic discrimination. The finding that Black adults themselves are among the more skeptical groups (27% say well represented, 34% say not well represented) suggests that those most affected by potential bias are most aware of it. Hispanic adults show a similar pattern: only 17% of the general public says Hispanic perspectives are well represented, while 39% say they are not.
key_points.verbatim: % of U.S. adults who say they think the people who design artificial intelligence (AI) computer programs take into account the experiences and views of Black adults à Very/Somewhat well 19 Not too/Not at all well 38 Not sure 42

key_points.point: The public is more worried than experts about AI leading to less human connection, with 57% of the public highly concerned versus 37% of experts. This reflects the skeptic belief that AI causes measurable social and psychological harms beyond economic displacement. The document presents this as a dimension of AI's negative impact on human relationships and community. This concern is distinct from economic or bias-related harms.
key_points.verbatim: The public is more worried about loss of human connection. While 57% of the public is highly concerned about AI leading to less connection between people, this drops to 37% among the experts we surveyed.
key_points.excerpt_context: Concerns section, page 13

key_points.point: Inaccurate information, impersonation, and data misuse are documented concerns for both experts and the public, with 66-70% highly concerned about AI-generated misinformation. This reflects the skeptic belief that AI causes immediate, measurable harms through unreliable and potentially deceptive outputs. The document presents these as current, not merely hypothetical, concerns. The high concern levels across both groups suggest these are perceived as present-tense problems.
key_points.verbatim: Inaccurate information, impersonation and data misuse are common worries for both experts and the public. For example, 66% of adults overall and 70% of experts are highly concerned about people getting inaccurate information from AI.
key_points.excerpt_context: Concerns section, page 13

key_points.point: The public's experiences with chatbots are significantly less positive than experts', with only 33% of public chatbot users finding them extremely or very helpful versus 61% of expert users. This reflects the skeptic belief that AI's benefits are unevenly distributed and that real-world performance falls short of promotional claims for ordinary users. The gap suggests AI tools are more useful to those with technical expertise. This is consistent with the jagged technological frontier concept.
key_points.verbatim: About six-in-ten AI experts who have used a chatbot (61%) say it was extremely or very helpful to them. Smaller shares of users in the general public (33%) say this. U.S. adults who've used chatbots are more likely than experts surveyed to say these tools have been not too or not at all helpful (21% vs. 9%).
key_points.excerpt_context: Chapter 1 / Chatbot use section, page 21-22

key_points.point: The public's concerns about AI have grown since 2021, with 51% of U.S. adults now more concerned than excited about AI versus only 15% of experts. This reflects the skeptic belief that public awareness of AI's harms is increasing over time as the technology becomes more prevalent. The document frames this as a trend, not a static snapshot. The growing concern gap between public and experts is itself a significant empirical finding.
key_points.verbatim: By contrast, U.S. adults as a whole — whose concerns over AI have grown since 2021 — are more inclined than experts to say they're more concerned than excited (51% vs. 15% among experts).
key_points.excerpt_context: Key findings section, page 7

key_points.point: The document records expert calls for more diverse AI workforces to counteract bias, reflecting the skeptic desire to ensure equitable AI development. These calls are presented alongside the observation that companies are scaling back diversity initiatives, creating tension between the desire and current industry practice. The document frames workforce diversity as a mechanism for reducing AI bias. This connects representation in AI design to downstream fairness outcomes.
key_points.verbatim: There are also growing calls for more diverse workforces to counteract bias. These efforts, though, have been met with pushback as companies scale back these initiatives.
key_points.excerpt_context: Bias and representation section, page 13

key_points.point: Both the public and experts want more personal control over AI in their lives, with 55% of adults and 57% of experts expressing this desire. This reflects the skeptic desire to safeguard individual autonomy and rights against AI's encroachment. The document notes ongoing debates about the difficulty or inability to opt out of AI. This desire for control is framed as a response to AI's pervasive and often invisible presence in daily life.
key_points.verbatim: Debates have continued around the difficulty or inability to opt out of AI. On balance, both the American public and the AI experts we surveyed want more control over this technology.
key_points.excerpt_context: Chapter 1 / Control section, page 22

key_points.point: The Pew Research Center study is explicitly designed to generate empirical evidence about AI's real-world impacts by surveying both the public and experts, reflecting the skeptic intention to ground AI policy in documented, measurable evidence rather than speculation. The methodology prioritizes representative sampling and in-depth interviews to capture diverse perspectives. This approach supports the skeptic argument that policy should respond to proven harms. The study's focus on jobs, bias, and regulation reflects skeptic priority areas.
key_points.verbatim: Pew Research Center conducted this study to understand how Americans' views of artificial intelligence compare with the views of those who have expertise in the field. This report includes findings from a survey of U.S. adults, a survey of AI experts and a series of in-depth interviews with experts.
key_points.excerpt_context: How we did this section, page 3

key_points.point: Expert quotes from Black and Hispanic researchers explicitly argue that underrepresented groups lack a seat at the table in AI design and will be disproportionately harmed by AI-driven displacement. This reflects the skeptic intention to center social and human-centric impacts in AI discourse. The quotes function as qualitative evidence of structural exclusion in the AI field. This framing connects workforce diversity to downstream harm prevention.
key_points.verbatim: We do not have any African Americans in the department at all … we need to bring these people in so they have a seat at the table. … If it's the same person over and over again … that is very narrow-minded ... I wish that there were more representation, and they would put more focus on that.
key_points.excerpt_context: Expert quotes / Bias and representation section, page 15

key_points.point: The document records widespread concern — across both the public and experts — about insufficient government regulation of AI, and low confidence in both government and industry to manage AI responsibly. This reflects the skeptic intention to advocate for public interest AI governance over industry self-regulation. The finding that even industry experts lack confidence in corporate responsibility strengthens this argument. The document implicitly supports calls for stronger democratic accountability in AI governance.
key_points.verbatim: They are also largely skeptical of industry efforts around responsible AI: 59% of the public and 55% of surveyed experts have not too much or no confidence in U.S. companies to develop and use AI responsibly.
key_points.excerpt_context: Regulation section, page 17

key_points.point: The document highlights that AI experts at colleges and universities are far more skeptical of corporate AI responsibility than their industry peers, suggesting that independent academic oversight is a necessary check on industry. This reflects the skeptic intention to institutionalize external accountability for AI development. The 21-percentage-point gap (60% vs. 39% lacking confidence) is presented as a significant structural finding. This supports arguments for independent algorithmic accountability mechanisms.
key_points.verbatim: Six-in-ten experts at colleges or universities have little to no confidence in U.S. companies to responsibly develop and use AI, versus 39% of those at private companies or businesses who say this.
key_points.excerpt_context: Key findings section, page 9-10

key_points.point: The racial and ethnic makeup of the AI expert field is itself a documented problem: the Pew survey did not receive enough responses from Hispanic or Black experts to report their views separately, reflecting the structural underrepresentation of these groups in the AI profession. This is an empirical finding about who constitutes the AI expert community. The document acknowledges this as a limitation of the study that mirrors a real-world diversity gap. This finding supports skeptic arguments about homogeneous AI development.
key_points.verbatim: We did not receive enough responses from Hispanic or Black experts to be able to report expert views by race and ethnicity; this reflects the racial and ethnic makeup of the field.
key_points.excerpt_context: Who did we define as AI experts section, page 11

key_points.point: The public is more worried than experts about AI-related job loss, with 56% of the public extremely or very concerned versus 25% of experts. This gap reflects the skeptic belief that ordinary workers bear the brunt of AI's labor displacement while experts — who benefit from AI — are insulated from its harms. The document presents this as a structural divide in who experiences AI's costs. This asymmetry of concern maps onto asymmetries of economic exposure.
key_points.verbatim: Continuing the theme on jobs, we find the public more anxious than experts about job loss (56% vs. 25% are extremely or very concerned).
key_points.excerpt_context: Concerns section, page 13

key_points.point: The document reports that 64% of U.S. adults believe AI will lead to fewer jobs over the next 20 years, while only 5% think it will lead to more jobs. This reflects widespread public belief in AI-driven labor displacement, a core skeptic concern. The contrast with expert views (39% predicting fewer jobs) shows that the public is more pessimistic about net job loss than domain experts. The caveat is that these are 20-year predictions, not current measurements.
key_points.verbatim: Overall, 64% of U.S. adults say that over the next 20 years, AI will lead to fewer jobs in the U.S., while just 5% think it will lead to more jobs.
key_points.excerpt_context: Section 3, page 44-45, paragraph on job predictions

key_points.point: The document reports that both the public and AI experts expect significant job losses for cashiers (73% each), factory workers (60%+), and journalists (59-60%), while AI experts are more pessimistic than the public about truck drivers (62% vs. 33%) and lawyers (38% vs. 23%). This reflects the skeptic belief that AI-driven displacement is shifting from low-skill to high-skill and knowledge-work professions. The convergence of expert and public views on journalism is particularly notable. The caveat is that these are predictions, not documented displacements.
key_points.verbatim: AI experts are more pessimistic about legal fields: 38% of AI experts say AI will lead to fewer jobs for lawyers, while 23% of the general public agrees.
key_points.excerpt_context: Section 3, page 47, paragraph on legal field job predictions

key_points.point: An AI expert quoted in the document explicitly states that AI is creating far fewer jobs than it destroys, estimating a ratio of 10 new jobs for every 1,000 eliminated, and specifically names truck drivers as a profession likely to disappear within 10-20 years. This is a direct skeptic claim about AI's complex and net-negative effects on the workforce. The expert also questions what displaced workers will do, raising concerns about social dislocation. This qualitative evidence reinforces the quantitative survey findings.
key_points.verbatim: ô[AI] is going to take over a lot of jobs. Of course itÆs creating new jobs, but that doesnÆt mean itÆs matching that. WeÆre generating maybe 10 jobs, but at the same time, weÆre taking away 1,000 jobs. For example, truck drivers, theyÆll be gone in 10, 20 years probably, if you think. Are we going to replace them? What are they going to do?ö
key_points.excerpt_context: Section 3, page 47, expert quote on job loss

key_points.point: The document reports consistent gender gaps in AI optimism among both experts and the general public, with men more optimistic than women across nearly all sectors including jobs, economy, education, environment, and medical care. Among experts, 68% of men vs. 42% of women expect AI to positively affect K-12 education; 43% of men vs. 18% of women expect positive environmental impacts. This aligns with the skeptic belief that AI's perceived benefits are unevenly distributed by gender. The caveat is that the survey measures optimism, not actual differential impact.
key_points.verbatim: There are sizable gender differences among experts in their views about AIÆs impact on certain aspects of society. For example, 68% of male experts surveyed say AIÆs impact on K-12 education over the next 20 years will be very or somewhat positive, compared with 42% of female experts.
key_points.excerpt_context: Section 3, page 43, paragraph on gender differences among experts

key_points.point: The document reports that 56% of AI experts and 51% of the public predict AI will negatively affect the news people receive, and 61% of experts believe AI will harm elections. These findings document expert-level concern about AI's harmful effects on information ecosystems and democratic processes. Skeptics would cite these figures as evidence of AI's immediate and measurable societal harms. The caveat is that these are predictions about future harm, not documentation of current harm.
key_points.verbatim: About half or more of experts (56%) and the public (51%) predict it will negatively affect the news people get.
key_points.excerpt_context: Section 3, page 42, paragraph on news impact

key_points.point: The document notes that the public is more pessimistic than experts about AI's impact on teachers (43% vs. 31% predicting fewer jobs) and medical doctors, while experts are more pessimistic about lawyers and truck drivers. This uneven pattern of concern across occupations reflects the skeptic belief in AI's jagged technological frontier — excelling in some domains while leaving others relatively unaffected. The divergence between expert and public views on specific occupations suggests that proximity to AI shapes risk perception. The caveat is that neither group has perfect predictive accuracy.
key_points.verbatim: The public is more pessimistic about medical doctors and teachers than AI experts. For example, 43% of adults overall say AI will lead to fewer teacher jobs in the next 20 years, compared with 31% of experts.
key_points.excerpt_context: Section 3, page 47, paragraph on teacher and doctor job predictions

key_points.point: The document notes that prior Pew research has documented anxiety about AI and jobs among both the public and workers, and the current survey confirms this sentiment is more widely held among the general public than among AI experts. This reflects the skeptic desire to protect human jobs from automation and to take public anxiety about displacement seriously as a policy signal. The document frames this as a persistent finding across multiple surveys. The caveat is that the document does not advocate for specific protective policies.
key_points.verbatim: WeÆve seen anxiety in our prior work around AI and jobs both among the public and workers. Our current survey finds this sentiment is more widely held among the general public than among AI experts.
key_points.excerpt_context: Section 3, page 44, paragraph introducing job predictions

key_points.point: The document reports that only 6% of Americans believe AI is highly likely to make humans happier, and about half say this is unlikely. Even among AI experts, more say happiness gains are unlikely (35%) than likely (22%). This finding challenges both accelerationist and safetyist framings by suggesting that neither the promise of abundance nor the fear of catastrophe dominates public or expert sentiment — instead, a pervasive skepticism about AI's human benefits prevails. The caveat is that 'happiness' is a broad and subjective outcome measure.
key_points.verbatim: Just 6% of Americans overall believe it is highly likely that AI will make humans happier. About half say this is unlikely.
key_points.excerpt_context: Section 3, page 48-49, paragraph on AI and human happiness

key_points.point: The document's survey methodology deliberately includes conferences focused on AI ethics, fairness, accountability, and social science implications, ensuring that skeptic and critical perspectives are represented in the expert sample. This methodological choice reflects an intention to ground AI impact assessment in real, present concerns rather than purely technical or accelerationist framings. The inclusion of FAccT, AIES, EAAMO, and the Summit on AI and Democracy in the sampling frame is particularly notable. The caveat is that the survey still cannot guarantee proportional representation of critical voices.
key_points.verbatim: These conferences cover topics related to artificial intelligence, including research, development, application, and ethical and social science implications. The list was developed in consultation with external advisers on the project and was designed to capture as diverse and wide a range of perspectives on AI as possible.
key_points.excerpt_context: Section 3, page 58-59, methodology paragraph on conference selection

key_points.point: The document reports that both the public and AI experts expect significant job losses for journalists (59-60%), and AI experts are more pessimistic than the public about lawyers (38% vs. 23%). This reflects the skeptic belief that AI disproportionately disrupts cognitive and white-collar labor, not just manual or routine work. The document explicitly notes that generative AI advances suggest fields requiring advanced degrees may see major impacts. The caveat is that these are forward-looking predictions.
key_points.verbatim: But advances in generative AI suggest that fields that have required advanced degrees, like law or engineering, may also see major impacts.
key_points.excerpt_context: Section 3, page 46, paragraph on occupational impacts

key_points.point: The document reports that the general public is substantially more uncertain than AI experts about AI's impact across multiple domains, with about one-in-five or more adults unsure about AI's effects on mental health therapists (26%), truck drivers (21%), and journalists (19%). This uncertainty is itself a significant finding for skeptic analysis, as it suggests that public risk perception is not simply alarmist but also reflects genuine informational gaps. The caveat is that uncertainty could cut in either direction — toward greater or lesser concern.
key_points.verbatim: The public is generally more likely than AI experts to say they are unsure about AIÆs impact on the number of jobs in these industries. For instance, about one-in-five or more U.S. adults say they are unsure of the type of impact AI will have on mental health therapists (26%), truck drivers (21%) or journalists (19%).
key_points.excerpt_context: Section 3, page 47, paragraph on public uncertainty

key_points.point: The survey's explicit focus on representation of different racial, ethnic, and gender groups in AI design reflects a desire to ensure AI development does not concentrate power or perpetuate inequality. The finding that women AI experts are far more critical of women's representation in AI design (64% say not well represented) than men (31%) illustrates how demographic homogeneity in the AI workforce translates into perceived design bias. For skeptics, this data supports calls for diversifying the AI workforce as a concrete mechanism for reducing bias. The advisory board's inclusion of a Data Equity Lead from the Aspen Institute signals institutional alignment with this goal.
key_points.verbatim: In line with the goals of the project, a roughly equal number of participants across race and ethnicity (White, Black, Hispanic, Asian) and gender (men and women) were selected, along with a mix of job sectors.
key_points.excerpt_context: Section on in-depth interviews, interview recruitment subsection

key_points.point: The survey notes that not enough responses were received from Hispanic or Black experts to report their views separately, reflecting the racial and ethnic makeup of the AI field. This data gap itself is a form of evidence: the underrepresentation of minority groups in the AI expert community means their perspectives are structurally absent from the data used to understand AI's impacts. For skeptics, this is a concrete illustration of how information and expertise asymmetry operates in AI governance. The note that 'these groups' responses are incorporated into the general figures' means their distinct views are effectively invisible in the aggregate data.
key_points.verbatim: We did not receive enough responses from Hispanic or Black experts to be able to report expert views by race and ethnicity; this reflects the racial and ethnic makeup of the field.
key_points.excerpt_context: Appendix B, note at end of Views of personal benefit versus harm from AI tables

key_points.point: 55% of U.S. adults say they would like more control over how AI is used in their lives, while only 19% are comfortable with their current level of control. This strong majority desire for greater personal control over AI reflects the skeptic concern that AI deployment is happening without adequate individual consent or agency. The finding that 59% of adults report having 'not too much' or 'no' control over AI in their lives (41% not too much, 18% none) quantifies the scale of this perceived powerlessness. For skeptics, this data supports arguments for stronger data rights, opt-out mechanisms, and transparency requirements.

key_points.excerpt_context: Topline: U.S. adults, AICONTROL2 question

The combined negative rating (34%) exceeds the combined positive rating (24%), suggesting the public is more worried than hopeful about AI in schools. For skeptics, this reflects concern about AI's potential to harm learning, exacerbate educational inequalities, or replace human teachers. This aligns with documented skeptic concerns about AI-driven cognitive atrophy and the erosion of genuine learning.

The large 'not sure' category (22%) and the 'equally positive and negative' category (26%) suggest the public has not internalized either optimistic or pessimistic narratives about AI's economic effects. For skeptics, the net-negative lean (31% negative vs. 22% positive) reflects public awareness of job displacement and economic disruption risks. This contrasts with accelerationist claims about AI-driven economic abundance.

key_points.point: The survey's in-depth interview component explicitly covered 'Representation among AI designers' and 'Bias in AI' as core topics, and the research team deliberately recruited participants across race, ethnicity, and gender dimensions. This methodological choice reflects an institutional belief that AI bias and representation are empirically important and measurable phenomena. The matching of moderators to participants by race (White, Black, Asian experts matched with same-race moderators; Hispanic experts with Hispanic moderators) reflects a commitment to reducing interviewer effects on sensitive topics. For skeptics, this design choice validates the importance of demographic representation in AI research itself.
key_points.verbatim: White, Black and Asian experts were matched with moderators of the same race as them. Hispanic experts were matched with a Hispanic moderator.
key_points.excerpt_context: Section on in-depth interviews, Interviews subsection

key_points.point: The Pew Research Center used race-matched moderators for in-depth interviews with AI experts, pairing White, Black, and Asian experts with same-race moderators and Hispanic experts with a Hispanic moderator. This methodological choice reflects an intention to reduce social desirability bias and create conditions where experts from underrepresented groups feel comfortable discussing sensitive topics like bias and representation. For skeptics, this approach models how research on AI bias should be conducted — with attention to the social dynamics that shape what people are willing to say. It also implicitly acknowledges that race and ethnicity affect how people experience and discuss AI.
key_points.verbatim: Four professional moderators conducted the online interviews in English on behalf of SSRS and Pew Research Center. White, Black and Asian experts were matched with moderators of the same race as them. Hispanic experts were matched with a Hispanic moderator.
key_points.excerpt_context: Section on in-depth interviews, Interviews subsection

For skeptics, this models how AI oversight bodies should be constituted — with explicit representation of equity and ethics expertise alongside technical expertise. The board's feedback on sample design and questionnaire design means equity concerns shaped the research instrument itself.

unmapped_concepts.suggested_description:
A situation concept that describes the systematic divergence between how AI experts and the general public perceive AI's risks, benefits, and prevalence.
Encompasses: Gaps in optimism about AI's societal impact, personal benefit expectations, job loss fears, chatbot helpfulness ratings, and perceived frequency of AI interaction.
Excludes: Gaps between different expert subgroups (e.g., academic vs. industry), which are covered by sector-based confidence findings; and gaps between political parties, which are covered by partisan AI regulation concepts.
unmapped_concepts.concept: The Pew survey documents a consistent and large divergence between AI experts and the U.S. public across nearly every dimension measured: optimism about AI's societal impact (56% vs. 17%), personal benefit expectations (76% vs. 24%), job loss fears (39% vs. 64%), and chatbot helpfulness (61% vs. 33%). This gap is not merely about information — experts believe the public interacts with AI far more than the public self-reports (79% vs. 27%). The gap functions as a structural feature of AI discourse, shaping how different actors interpret the same technology.
unmapped_concepts.reason: No existing taxonomy node captures the systematic, multi-dimensional divergence between expert and public AI perceptions as a situation concept. This gap is central to the document's argument and has distinct implications for each POV camp.
unmapped_concepts.Accelerationist Interpretation: Accelerationists read the expert-public gap as evidence that the public is misinformed or lacks the technical literacy to appreciate AI's transformative potential. They argue that expert optimism should guide policy, not public anxiety. Closing the gap means educating the public, not slowing AI development.
unmapped_concepts.Safetyist Interpretation: Safetyists see the gap as a warning sign: experts who benefit from AI are systematically less worried about its risks than those who will bear its costs. The gap between expert and public concern about job loss (25% vs. 56%) and human connection (37% vs. 57%) suggests that expert-led governance may systematically underweight public harms.
unmapped_concepts.Skeptic Interpretation: Skeptics argue the gap reflects a structural conflict of interest: AI experts are insulated from AI's harms and overexposed to its benefits, making them unreliable guides for public policy. The fact that even experts who use chatbots daily rate them as less helpful than they claim (33% of public users vs. 61% of expert users) suggests that expert enthusiasm does not translate to public value.
